title: Pre-Islamic Arabia
subtitle: Context and sources
overview: Western Arabia contained polytheistic communities, Jewish groups, and diverse Christian traditions. The Qur’an engages Jewish and Christian themes, but the precise religious landscape of sixth-century Mecca is debated.
method: Distinguish archaeological and external evidence from later literary accounts. Do not assume every feature of later sīrah describes the sixth century.
response: The biblical question concerns continuity with earlier revelation, not merely cultural similarities.
sources: Fred Donner, Muhammad and the Believers; Robert Hoyland, Seeing Islam as Others Saw It

title: Muhammad’s Life
subtitle: Traditional biography and historical method
overview: Traditional chronology places Muhammad’s birth around 570, first revelation around 610, emigration to Medina in 622, conquest of Mecca in 630, and death in 632. The Qur’an is early but not a continuous biography; fuller narratives survive in later sīrah and hadith collections.
method: Classify reports as Qur’anic, early external testimony, later sīrah, or hadith; compare independent attestations before affirming details.
response: Deuteronomy 13:1–5 and 18:20–22 are Christian tests for prophetic claims, not descriptions written about Muhammad.
sources: Ibn Hisham, Sīrah; Sean Anthony, Muhammad and the Empires of Faith

title: Muhammad’s Prophetic Claims
subtitle: Revelation and biblical tests
overview: Islamic tradition identifies Gabriel as the mediator of Muhammad’s revelations. The Qur’an claims divine origin and presents Muhammad as messenger and seal of the prophets. The historical occurrence of a reported experience and its divine interpretation are distinct questions.
method: Avoid arguing that Paul predicted Muhammad. Instead evaluate the general principle that a later angelic message cannot overturn the apostolic gospel.
response: Compare Qur’anic denial of divine Sonship and crucifixion with John 1:1–14 and 1 Corinthians 15:3–8.

title: Compilation of the Qur’an
subtitle: Abu Bakr and Uthman
overview: Bukhari 4986 reports Zayd ibn Thabit collecting Qur’anic material under Abu Bakr after losses among reciters. Bukhari 4987 describes Uthman commissioning standard copies and ordering other written materials destroyed. These are later transmitted accounts of seventh-century events.
method: Distinguish the traditional account from manuscript-supported reconstruction. Standardization is neither automatic proof of corruption nor proof of verbatim preservation of every prior reading.
response: Textual preservation and divine inspiration are separate questions.
sources: Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Virtues of the Qur’an; François Déroche, The One and the Many

title: Early Qur’anic Manuscripts
subtitle: Material evidence
overview: The Birmingham folios preserve portions of surahs 18–20; radiocarbon dating concerns parchment, not the precise writing date. The Sana’a palimpsest has an erased lower text with variants. Early codices help reconstruct the development of the consonantal text.
references: Birmingham Mingana Islamic Arabic 1572a; Sana’a palimpsest; Codex Parisino-petropolitanus
method: Compare orthography, consonantal differences, dating methods and provenance. Do not equate every spelling difference with a changed theological message.
response: Historical manuscript evidence can test claims of transmission, but cannot independently establish divine origin.
sources: University of Birmingham manuscript collection; Marijn van Putten, Quranic Arabic

title: Qirāʾāt and Aḥruf
subtitle: Reading traditions
overview: Canonical qirāʾāt are transmitted recitational traditions; aḥruf are a separate category discussed in hadith and classical theory. Differences may concern vowels, consonants, grammar, or meaning. The familiar Hafs-from-Asim reading is one widespread transmission.
method: Do not equate seven aḥruf with the seven canonical readings. Distinguish readings permitted by a rasm from readings that require consonantal differences.
response: A claim of perfect preservation must define whether it concerns consonants, every canonical reading, or a single modern printed edition.
sources: Ibn al-Jazari, al-Nashr; Shady Nasser, The Transmission of the Variant Readings

title: Hadith and Historical Reliability
subtitle: Transmission and verification
overview: A hadith commonly includes isnad (transmission chain) and matn (content). Sunni grading assesses transmitter reliability and continuity. Modern historical methods also examine common links, literary dependence and corroboration.
references: Sahih al-Bukhari, opening Revelation reports; Bukhari 4986–4987
method: Traditional sahih classification and independent historical demonstration are not identical. Late compilation dates do not establish late invention of every report.
response: A Christian assessment should engage reports accurately without presupposing their historical authenticity or falsity.
sources: Jonathan Brown, Hadith; Harald Motzki, studies in hadith dating

title: Qur’an and Biblical Revelation
subtitle: Competing Christologies
overview: The Qur’an calls Jesus Messiah and affirms his virgin birth but rejects identifying him with God (5:72), saying Three (4:171), and the standard Christian crucifixion account (4:157). The New Testament presents Christ as eternal Word and proclaims his death and resurrection.
method: Compare texts in context. Do not say the Qur’an explicitly defines the Trinity as Father, Son, and Mary; 5:116 does not give that formal definition.
response: The disagreement concerns revelation, identity of Christ, and redemption; not simply terminology.

title: Presuppositional Evaluation
subtitle: Authority and worldview coherence
overview: Van Til emphasizes the self-attesting triune God and rejection of autonomous neutrality. Bavinck emphasizes the organic unity of divine revelation. Bahnsen develops transcendental critique of rival worldviews. Their emphases should be distinguished.
method: Ask which revelation supplies the ultimate standard and assess concrete historical and theological claims. Do not claim that Muslims cannot reason or that every Islamic view has been disproved by assertion.
response: From a confessional Reformed Baptist standpoint, Scripture is the final written authority and Christ the climactic revelation.
sources: 1689 Confession chs. 1, 2, 8; Van Til, Christian Apologetics; Bavinck, Reformed Dogmatics; Bahnsen, Always Ready
